ranking.rationale: Age is one of the most robust cross-state predictors of mobility: residential moving behavior varies strongly over the life course and this relationship is semantically stable across states. It adds broad signal without relying heavily on geography-specific labor markets, racial composition, or other brittle distributional shortcuts.

Educational attainment is one of the most robust cross-state predictors of mobility-related outcomes in ACS: it captures human capital and life-course position beyond age, is broadly comparable across states, and is less tied to local geographic artifacts than commute, income, ancestry, or race variables.

Employment status adds strong, broadly state-stable signal for mobility beyond age and education because labor-force attachment is tightly linked to whether and why people move, while being less geography-specific and less shortcut-prone than race, ancestry, income, commute, or citizenship-related variables.

Personal income adds strong, broadly state-stable signal for mobility beyond age, education, and employment status because residential mobility is tightly linked to economic resources and labor-market opportunity. It is more semantically tied to the decision or ability to move than demographic shortcut variables like race, sex, ancestry, or citizenship, and less geographically brittle than commute time. It also complements ESR by capturing within-employment heterogeneity that remains predictive across states.

Usual hours worked adds strong, broadly state-invariant signal about labor-force attachment and job intensity beyond employment status and income. It is directly relevant to mobility/commuting behavior, complements ESR and PINCP without relying on geography or sensitive demographic proxies, and should generalize more stably across states than race, ancestry, citizenship, sex, or commute-time variables.

Class of worker adds strong, broadly state-stable signal about labor-market attachment and job structure beyond age, education, employment status, income, and hours. It is more semantically tied to mobility outcomes than demographic shortcut variables like race or sex, and less geography-specific than commute time or ancestry-related features.

Relationship to householder adds strong, broadly state-stable signal about life stage and household role that is highly relevant to mobility while being less geography-specific than ancestry, race, or citizenship proxies. It complements age, education, employment, income, hours, and class of worker by capturing whether someone is the householder, spouse, child, or other relative/nonrelative, which helps distinguish structurally different mobility patterns without relying on brittle state-specific composition effects.

Marital status adds broadly stable signal for mobility beyond age, education, income, work hours, class of worker, employment, and relationship: it captures household formation and family-tied moving behavior that generalizes across states. It is less geography-specific and less likely to act as a brittle demographic proxy than ancestry, race, nativity, or citizenship, and more broadly applicable than child- or disability-specific variables.

Disability status adds broadly state-stable signal for mobility through functional limitations and labor-market attachment, complementing age, education, employment, hours, income, relationship, and marital status. It is more semantically tied to moving difficulty than sex or commute time, and less likely than ancestry, race, nativity, or citizenship to act as a geography-dependent demographic shortcut.

Cognitive difficulty is a broadly state-stable indicator of functional limitation that should add mobility-relevant signal beyond age, disability, work, income, and education. It is less likely than race, ancestry, nativity, or sex to act mainly as a geographic or demographic shortcut, and more directly tied to the task than niche household variables or commute time.

Commute time adds strong, broadly state-stable signal about work attachment and residential mobility constraints beyond employment status, hours, class of worker, income, and demographics. It is more semantically tied to mobility behavior than ancestry, race, sex, or citizenship variables, which are more prone to acting as demographic or geography-linked shortcuts.

Citizenship status adds broadly stable signal for mobility through migration history, legal status, and labor-market attachment that should generalize across states. It is less geographically brittle than ancestry or race, more relevant for adults than parent/grandparent-child household variables, and more informative than sex once age, education, employment, income, hours, and commute are already included.

Nativity adds broadly stable signal for mobility through migration history, assimilation, and labor-market sorting that should generalize across states better than race, ancestry, or sex. It is less geographically brittle than ancestry/race proxies and more relevant across the adult ACS mobility population than niche household-structure variables or rare disability indicators, while still contributing information not fully captured by citizenship, education, income, and employment features already selected.

Hearing difficulty adds individual functional-limitation signal that is plausibly relevant to mobility and should transfer across states. It is less geography-encoded and less likely than race, ancestry, or sex to act mainly as a demographic shortcut, while also being more broadly applicable than child- or grandparent-specific variables and less sparse/state-specific than military status.

Vision difficulty adds broadly stable signal about disability-related functional limitation that is relevant to mobility and complements already selected hearing difficulty and general disability status. It is less geography-specific and less likely than sex, race, ancestry, or military variables to act mainly as a demographic shortcut or state-specific artifact.

Sex adds broad, state-stable signal for mobility through life-course, labor-market, and household-role differences not fully captured by age, education, marital status, work, and relationship variables. It is generally more portable across states than ancestry or race, less niche than military/grandparent-care variables, and more broadly applicable than parent-employment status.

Military service status adds plausible, state-stable signal for mobility through veteran/active-duty life-course and relocation patterns, while being less likely than ancestry or race to act as a demographic shortcut and more broadly informative than niche household-structure variables like ESP or GCL given the features already selected.

GCL adds household structure and caregiving responsibility information that is plausibly linked to mobility and remains fairly stable across states, while being less redundant with already selected age/marital/relationship/employment features than ESP and less likely than ANC or RAC1P to act as demographic or geography proxies.

ESP is weak and often not applicable, but it can still add some stable household-context signal for mobility beyond age, relationship, marital status, and employment. ANC and RAC1P are more likely to act as demographic/geographic shortcuts whose predictive patterns vary across states, so they are less desirable for OOD generalization.

Ancestry can add some residual signal about migration and household/community ties beyond nativity, citizenship, language, and race, while being somewhat more behaviorally linked to mobility than race alone. Both are shortcut-prone, but RAC1P is more likely to encode unstable state-specific demographic composition and structural disparities rather than portable mechanisms, so ANC has slightly better marginal stable value.

Race can add some residual predictive signal for mobility through persistent structural inequalities not fully captured by education, income, employment, nativity, ancestry, and language, but it is weaker and less stability-favored than the already selected socioeconomic features because it can act as a demographic shortcut and reflect state-specific composition. As the only remaining candidate, it provides the last marginal information.

llm_calls.content: {"selected_feature_id":10,"rationale":"Relationship to householder adds strong, broadly state-stable signal about life stage and household role that is highly relevant to mobility while being less geography-specific than ancestry, race, or citizenship proxies. It complements age, education, employment, income, hours, and class of worker by capturing whether someone is the householder, spouse, child, or other relative/nonrelative, which helps distinguish structurally different mobility patterns without relying on brittle state-specific composition effects."}

{"selected_feature_id":2,"rationale":"Marital status adds broadly stable signal for mobility beyond age, education, income, work hours, class of worker, employment, and relationship: it captures household formation and family-tied moving behavior that generalizes across states. It is less geography-specific and less likely to act as a brittle demographic proxy than ancestry, race, nativity, or citizenship, and more broadly applicable than child- or disability-specific variables."}

{"selected_feature_id":4,"rationale":"Disability status adds broadly state-stable signal for mobility through functional limitations and labor-market attachment, complementing age, education, employment, hours, income, relationship, and marital status. It is more semantically tied to moving difficulty than sex or commute time, and less likely than ancestry, race, nativity, or citizenship to act as a geography-dependent demographic shortcut."}

{"selected_feature_id":13,"rationale":"Cognitive difficulty is a broadly state-stable indicator of functional limitation that should add mobility-relevant signal beyond age, disability, work, income, and education. It is less likely than race, ancestry, nativity, or sex to act mainly as a geographic or demographic shortcut, and more directly tied to the task than niche household variables or commute time."}

{"selected_feature_id":6,"rationale":"Citizenship status adds broadly stable signal for mobility through migration history, legal status, and labor-market attachment that should generalize across states. It is less geographically brittle than ancestry or race, more relevant for adults than parent/grandparent-child household variables, and more informative than sex once age, education, employment, income, hours, and commute are already included."}

{"selected_feature_id":9,"rationale":"Nativity adds broadly stable signal for mobility through migration history, assimilation, and labor-market sorting that should generalize across states better than race, ancestry, or sex. It is less geographically brittle than ancestry/race proxies and more relevant across the adult ACS mobility population than niche household-structure variables or rare disability indicators, while still contributing information not fully captured by citizenship, education, income, and employment features already selected."}

{"selected_feature_id":11,"rationale":"Hearing difficulty adds individual functional-limitation signal that is plausibly relevant to mobility and should transfer across states. It is less geography-encoded and less likely than race, ancestry, or sex to act mainly as a demographic shortcut, while also being more broadly applicable than child- or grandparent-specific variables and less sparse/state-specific than military status."}

{"selected_feature_id":12,"rationale":"Vision difficulty adds broadly stable signal about disability-related functional limitation that is relevant to mobility and complements already selected hearing difficulty and general disability status. It is less geography-specific and less likely than sex, race, ancestry, or military variables to act mainly as a demographic shortcut or state-specific artifact."}

{"selected_feature_id":3,"rationale":"Sex adds broad, state-stable signal for mobility through life-course, labor-market, and household-role differences not fully captured by age, education, marital status, work, and relationship variables. It is generally more portable across states than ancestry or race, less niche than military/grandparent-care variables, and more broadly applicable than parent-employment status."}

{"selected_feature_id":7,"rationale":"Military service status adds plausible, state-stable signal for mobility through veteran/active-duty life-course and relocation patterns, while being less likely than ancestry or race to act as a demographic shortcut and more broadly informative than niche household-structure variables like ESP or GCL given the features already selected."}

{"selected_feature_id":15,"rationale":"GCL adds household structure and caregiving responsibility information that is plausibly linked to mobility and remains fairly stable across states, while being less redundant with already selected age/marital/relationship/employment features than ESP and less likely than ANC or RAC1P to act as demographic or geography proxies."}

{"selected_feature_id":5,"rationale":"ESP is weak and often not applicable, but it can still add some stable household-context signal for mobility beyond age, relationship, marital status, and employment. ANC and RAC1P are more likely to act as demographic/geographic shortcuts whose predictive patterns vary across states, so they are less desirable for OOD generalization."}

{"selected_feature_id":8,"rationale":"Ancestry can add some residual signal about migration and household/community ties beyond nativity, citizenship, language, and race, while being somewhat more behaviorally linked to mobility than race alone. Both are shortcut-prone, but RAC1P is more likely to encode unstable state-specific demographic composition and structural disparities rather than portable mechanisms, so ANC has slightly better marginal stable value."}

{"selected_feature_id":14,"rationale":"Race can add some residual predictive signal for mobility through persistent structural inequalities not fully captured by education, income, employment, nativity, ancestry, and language, but it is weaker and less stability-favored than the already selected socioeconomic features because it can act as a demographic shortcut and reflect state-specific composition. As the only remaining candidate, it provides the last marginal information."}
